citation: Feldges, Tom, and Sonia Pieczenko. "Boredom in Educational Contexts: A Critical Review." Encyclopaideia – Journal of Phenomenology and Education 24, no. 57 (2020): 1-15. https://doi.org/10.6092/issn.1825-8670/11035.
discipline: philosophy of education / educational phenomenology, reviewing educational-psychological and neuroscientific literatures on boredom
thesis: Reviewing psychological, neuroscientific, and educational-phenomenological (Husserl via Buck) approaches to boredom in schooling, the authors argue that Götz & Frenzel's (2006) influential four-type taxonomy of academic boredom conflates antecedent states, 'actual' boredom, and resultant/directed-emotion states, and that approaches driven mainly by a wish to control/avoid boredom foreclose asking whether boredom has a legitimate role in education and whether classroom boredom is largely an artifact of frontal-instruction pedagogy rather than intrinsic to learning.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates the topic via the claim that students experience boredom in roughly half of lessons; frames a third-person/naturalistic vs. first-person/phenomenological dichotomy (Nagel, Wittgenstein); previews bringing educational psychology (Götz & Frenzel, 2006) into conversation with Husserl and Buck.

sections.title: Defining and categorising boredom
sections.summary: Surveys competing definitions (Fenichel, Lipps, Pekrun); stages the mood-vs-emotion debate via a single FCM citation plus Being and Time, Schopenhauer, Bollnow, and Prinz; brackets trait-boredom in favor of state-boredom.

sections.title: Psychological and neuroscientific accounts of boredom
sections.summary: Lays out psychology's epistemological/ontological dilemma, the functional/regulatory account (Bench & Lench, 2013), autonomic-arousal measures (London et al., 1972), ECN/DMN neuroimaging (Danckert & Merrifield, 2018; Andrews-Hanna, 2012), and introduces Götz & Frenzel's four-type taxonomy of academic boredom.

sections.title: Phenomenology and the bored Self
sections.summary: Introduces Buck's Lernen und Erfahrung (learning as process of experiencing, not teleological endpoint), Marion's self-abandonment account, and three Husserlian building blocks: stream of consciousness, pure ego, and internal time-consciousness (retention/protention, subjective vs. cosmic time).

sections.title: What is it like to be bored?
sections.summary: Applies the Husserlian framework to each of Götz & Frenzel's four types: indifferent boredom as antecedent in-between stage; calibrating boredom as closest to genuine boredom; goal-seeking and reactant boredom as increasingly directed, escape-oriented emotion rather than the mood of boredom.

sections.title: Discussion
sections.summary: Argues the mood/emotion distinction is neglected in mainstream educational-psychological literature (Pekrun & Linnenbrink-Garcia's Handbook); reframes the question as whether boredom deserves 'a better reputation'; asks how much classroom boredom is produced by frontal instruction rather than intrinsic to schooling.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Restates the definitional impasse, the taxonomy critique, and the two open normative questions; closes on a bucket-vs-roof analogy contrasting symptom-management with structural critique of educational practice.

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form)
constructs.treatment: single citation of Heidegger's 'reveals being as a whole' passage, used only to establish mood-not-object-directedness; not developed further

constructs.label: situational vs. trait/state boredom
constructs.treatment: trait explicitly bracketed; state-boredom adopted as the paper's unit of analysis ('a token of experienced boredom')

constructs.label: boredom proneness
constructs.treatment: named only as the bracketed trait pole of the state/trait distinction; not independently theorized

constructs.label: mind-wandering / task-unrelated thought
constructs.treatment: Type-2 'calibrating boredom' glossed as free-roaming thought/mind-wandering, tied to the ECN-to-DMN switch

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: ECN deactivation as neural correlate of outward-attention withdrawal; mapped onto Husserl's pre-reflective vs. reflective self-given-ness distinction

constructs.label: boredom-as-regulatory-signal (functional account)
constructs.treatment: boredom has a functional purpose, informing the individual and motivating search for a more interesting environment/goal (Bench & Lench, 2013; Elpidorou, 2017)

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: indirect, via Kuh et al. (2008) student-engagement literature and a warning against over-stimulating 'edutrainer' pedagogy

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: grounded in Lipps's (1903) incitement-conflict definition of boredom

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: Husserl's retention/protention account; subjective time and 'cosmic' (objective) time diverge during a bored episode

measures.label: self-report / survey scale
measures.treatment: Götz & Frenzel's (2006) 'phenomenological' student interviews (qualitative self-report, not philosophical phenomenology); Vodanovich's (2003) psychometric-measures review cited

measures.label: heart rate / HRV
measures.treatment: London et al. (1972) autonomic arousal — skin-conductivity and heart-frequency changes as boredom-behaviour indices; noted as unclear where 'pure' boredom ends and resultant states begin

measures.label: general neuroimaging (DMN/ECN) — not an EEG-specific, pupillometric, or eye-tracking measure named in this source
measures.treatment: Danckert & Merrifield (2018) and Andrews-Hanna (2012) fMRI-adjacent Default Mode Network / Executive Control Network findings; DMN activation necessary but not sufficient for boredom (also occurs in meditative depersonalization)

readings.claim: No commonly agreed definition of boredom exists across psychological, neuroscientific, and phenomenological literatures; the concept is contested, complex, multidimensional and constructed.

Intentionality (object-directedness) distinguishes moods (boredom, anxiety) from emotions; mainstream educational-psychological literature neglects this distinction, treating moods as 'low-intensity emotions.'

ECN deactivation / DMN activation neuroimaging findings unexpectedly redescribe well onto the Husserlian outward-to-inward attention switch, a fit the authors call 'remarkable' since neuroscience usually is read as supporting cognitive psychology.
DMN activation is necessary but not sufficient for boredom, since it also occurs during meditation-induced depersonalization without boredom being present.

Götz & Frenzel's (2006) four-type taxonomy conflates an antecedent state (Type 1, indifferent boredom), a form closest to genuine boredom (Type 2, calibrating boredom), and resultant directed-emotion states (Types 3-4, goal-seeking and reactant boredom).

A taxonomy that folds antecedents, core boredom, and consequences into one label licenses treating the whole spectrum as something to be recognized, regulated, and controlled, foreclosing the question of boredom's potential legitimate role in education.

Buck's account of learning as a 'process of experiencing' (not a teleological/achievement endpoint) reframes boredom and frustration as revealing something about the structure of the educational encounter itself, not merely an obstacle to eliminate.

Two open normative questions: (a) does boredom deserve 'a better reputation' as intrinsic to institutionalized schooling; (b) how much classroom boredom is an artifact of frontal-instruction pedagogy rather than intrinsic to learning.
Closing bucket-vs-roof analogy: symptom-management (recognizing/controlling boredom) vs. structural critique (asking bigger questions about educational practice).

interlocutors.role: single-quote source for mood-not-object-directedness; not developed

interlocutors.name: Marion, Jean-Luc — Reduction and Givenness (1998)
interlocutors.role: contrast-foil for existential self-loss/abandonment in boredom

interlocutors.name: Fenichel, Otto (1953)
interlocutors.role: psychoanalytic definition of boredom (quiet vs. fidgety forms)

interlocutors.name: Lipps, Theodor (1903)
interlocutors.role: incitement-conflict definition of boredom, taken up via Fenichel

interlocutors.name: Schopenhauer, Arthur
interlocutors.role: boredom as will lacking an object; fearful emptiness

interlocutors.role: affirms boredom lacks a directed object, supporting the mood reading

interlocutors.name: Prinz, Jesse — Gut Reactions (2004)

interlocutors.name: Pekrun, Reinhard (2006; Pekrun et al., 2010; Pekrun & Linnenbrink-Garcia, 2015)
interlocutors.role: source of achievement-emotion / control-value framing, later critiqued for eliding mood/emotion distinction

interlocutors.role: source of the four-type taxonomy of academic boredom, the paper's central critical target

interlocutors.name: Danckert, James, & Merrifield, Colleen (2018)
interlocutors.role: ECN/DMN neuroimaging account of boredom and sustained attention

interlocutors.name: Andrews-Hanna, Jessica R. (2012)
interlocutors.role: Default Mode Network and internal mentation

interlocutors.name: Elpidorou, Andreas (2017)
interlocutors.role: regulatory theory of boredom; constructed/multidimensional character of the concept

interlocutors.role: cited on the difficulty of empirically bounding boredom's 'inherently internal experience'; likely Strand-C cluster author (bor-sec-20/26 range), not yet built at time of writing — note only

interlocutors.name: Nagel, Thomas — 'What is it like to be a bat?' (1979)
interlocutors.role: frames boredom as private, first-person-exclusive experience; structures §5's title

interlocutors.name: Nietzsche, Friedrich (via Pattison, 2013)
interlocutors.role: boredom as a statement about a task/society/world, not a report of inner state

interlocutors.name: Kierkegaard, Søren (via Pattison, 2013)
interlocutors.role: boredom as 'the root of all evil' — opening foil, not endorsed outright

tensions.axis: mood (non-intentional) vs. emotion (intentionally directed) — Prinz's intentionality criterion
tensions.note: phenomenological/philosophical camp (Heidegger, Schopenhauer, Bollnow, Prinz) treats boredom as a mood; educational-psychological literature (Pekrun, Götz & Hall) collapses the distinction, calling moods 'low-intensity emotions.'
Götz & Frenzel's four-type taxonomy is argued to conflate precursor (Type 1), core (Type 2), and consequence (Types 3-4) states under one label.
psychology's epistemological/ontological dilemma in accessing an 'inherently internal experience' empirically.

tensions.axis: teleological/achievement-endpoint view of learning vs. Buck's process-of-experiencing view
tensions.note: the functional-psychological undercurrent fixes attention on recognizing and controlling boredom as an obstacle to accomplishment.

tensions.axis: control-and-avoid orientation vs. critical-questioning orientation toward boredom's institutional role
tensions.note: whether boredom deserves 'a better reputation' as intrinsic to schooling, or should simply be eliminated.

tensions.axis: neuroscience aligning with phenomenology vs. with cognitive psychology
tensions.note: authors note it is 'remarkable' that DMN/ECN findings fit the phenomenological account, since neuroscience is usually read as supporting cognitive psychology instead.

fcm.note: Single verbatim citation of the profound-boredom passage ('reveals being as a whole') used solely to establish mood-not-object-directedness; no engagement with FCM's tripartite structure, the 'es ist einem langweilig' formula, or the Augenblick. Not a sustained reading of FCM (P/anticipatory-application).

dataset_channels.note: This source's discussed measures (self-report interviews, autonomic arousal/HR, general DMN/ECN neuroimaging) do not include EEG-specific, pupillometric, or gaze/eye-tracking channels; the VR Attention Study dataset is not yet built. Treat any linkage as provisional pending independent confirmation of measure-modality overlap (P/anticipatory-application).
